arXiv:2608.15402v1 [cs.LG] 15 Aug 2026

Towards a theory of inference-time alignment with
unknown rewards

Steve Hanneke   Hongao Wang   Mingyue Xu
Purdue University ††thanks: steve.hanneke@gmail.com††thanks: wang5270@purdue.edu††thanks: xu1864@purdue.edu
Abstract

Generative model alignment has received broad interest, and significant progress has been made in supervised fine-tuning and inference-time computation. Yet, alignment has remained poorly understood from a statistical learning perspective. We formulate inference-time alignment as a weak-to-strong learning problem, where a reference policy (weak learner) is assumed to be fairly good and the goal is to produce a strong learner that predicts a good response at test time with arbitrarily high probability. Our problem is formulated as learning from scratch — everything is learned from data rather than assuming access to a good reward estimate, and thus differs from the existing inference-time alignment theory. Our model shares similarity to the recent work of Joshi et al., [17], where for each prompt, there could be multiple good responses. Our definition of the alignment learnability follows the PAC learning principle. We introduce a novel combinatorial dimension of the reward class which we call the alignment dimension, and show that it completely characterizes the alignment learnability — a reward class is alignment learnable if and only if its alignment dimension is finite. The core of our learning procedure works by invoking the ordinary one-inclusion graph algorithm to run a tournament over all pairs of label sets satisfying that neither is a subset of the other. We believe our results might shed light on establishing a complete theoretical understanding towards alignment.

1 Introduction

Alignment — aligning AI agents to behave in accordance with humans intentions — is motivated from the observation that while modern generative models acquire impressive capabilities from scalable training, they may exhibit unintended or harmful behavior [3, 29]. Let us take the language model alignment as example.11 1 Throughout out the paper, we will take the language model alignment as example for presentation, it is worth emphasizing that our theory captures inference-time alignment in general for other generative models. Traditional methodology for language model alignment falls into two categories, namely, Reinforcement Learning from Human/AI Feedback (RLHF/RLAIF) [10, 48, 6, 20] and inference-time alignment [18, 36, 15]. RLHF/RLAIF methods usually involve two steps, where a parameterized reward function is first learned using the curated preference data annotated by human beings or AI, and is then used to optimize the model to produce responses that receive higher rewards. In contrast, inference-time alignment approaches work by selecting or steering the model’s generated responses according to a reward signal at inference time, and is thus free from updating the model parameters. We defer a detailed discussion of these two paradigms to Section 1.1.

Yet, despite its increasing popularity in both empirical and theoretical investigations, only a very few works have tried to model the alignment problem from a statistical learning perspective and explored its learning performance guarantee. In fact, theoretical works on RLHF have largely focused on designing better preference-optimization objectives, motivated by the empirical observation of the reward overoptimization (a.k.a. reward hacking) [13, 23, 16, 42]; or on deriving sample complexity guarantees under structured learning models, such as assuming linear rewards, log-linear policies, and contextual-bandit formulation [43, 28, 21, 12]. For inference-time alignment, existing theoretical researches have conditioned on a reward model satisfying prescribed accuracy or uncertainty assumptions [15, 7, 2, 34], rather than studying the end-to-end statistical problem of learning the reward model from finite preference data and subsequently using it to align unseen test instances. Motivated by this, we ask a more basic statistical learning question:

Question.

Which reward classes are learnable for inference-time alignment, with only access to the preference data?

In this work, we provide an answer to the above question by studying the problem of inference-time alignment from a statistical learning perspective. For simplicity, we call our problem alignment rather inference-time alignment and defer its formal definition to Section 2. As a pioneering work, we restrict to the basic setting where the reward class contains binary reward functions, i.e., ℛ⊆{0,1}𝒳×𝒴\mathcal{R}\subseteq\{0,1\}^{\mathcal{X}\times\mathcal{Y}} and assume that the true reward function lies in class, i.e., r∗∈ℛr^{*}\in\mathcal{R}. Unlike the existing routes, we formulate the alignment problem as a boosting/weak-to-strong learning problem, where the data is generated from a reference/base policy πref\pi_{\mathrm{ref}} whose performance is assumed to be fair, in a sense that it has a constant probability of generating a good response (with r∗r^{*} value 1) for a given input. Therefore, a reference policy can be thought of as a weak learner in the context of weak-to-strong learning. In practice, πref\pi_{\mathrm{ref}} is usually obtained from a pretrained language model or a supervised fine-tuning (SFT) model. For instance, InstructGPT uses the pretrained GPT-3 as the reference model [29].22 2 Other common reference models include the LLaMA series [38], the Gemma series [37], the Qwen series [4], etc. This is because pretrained models typically possess nice properties such as linguistic fluency and broad knowledge, but their pretraining does not pay much attention to following human instructions or preferences. On this account, practical language model alignment methods are usually designed to output selective responses generated from (some policy close to) πref\pi_{\mathrm{ref}}. The goal of alignment is to boost the performance of the reference model using the training data with human-annotated preferences. We adopt the classical (ϵ,δ)(\epsilon,\delta) standard of statistical learning to measure the performance, namely, with probability at least 1−δ1-\delta, the probability that the learner (aligned model) “predicts” a response with r∗r^{*} value 0 is at most ϵ\epsilon. Thus, the aligned model can be think of a stronger learner as the target of boosting. In particular, we consider inference-time alignment — the learner is expected to select a response with r∗r^{*} value 1 from multiple πref\pi_{\mathrm{ref}}-generated candidates with arbitrarily high probability at test time.

Our main contributions are summarized as follows. To our best knowledge, we are the first to develop a statistical learning framework for the general alignment problem, in particular inference-time alignment. Our problem is formulated as learning from scratch — everything is learned from data, which we call “inference-time alignment with unknown rewards”. This distinguishes our work from existing inference-time alignment theoretical works since they assume having access to a good reward estimate (see Section 1.1 for a detailed discussion). Although being superficially related to several existing statistical learning frameworks such as (i) multiclass learning — the learner outputs only one of the multiple labels for each test instance [26, 27] and (ii) list learning — the learner outputs multiple plausible labels for each instance rather than just one [9], we notice that our formulation differs from them — multiple labels might be correct but the learner only needs to find one of them. In fact, our learning framework is more close to the recent works of [17, 30] (see Section 1.1 for a detailed discussion), and might be of independent interest to the learning theory community. We propose a novel combinatorial dimension of the reward class, which we name the alignment dimension. We then provide a complete characterization on the learnability of the alignment problem, which we call the alignment learnability — any reward class is alignment learnable if and only if its alignment dimension is finite. We consider our work as an initial step towards establishing a statistical learning theory for the general alignment problem, potentially shedding light on developing more systematic principles for alignment in practice.

1.1 Related works

RLHF/RLAIF.

Reinforcement Learning from Human/AI Feedback (RLHF/RLAIF) framework is summarized as follows. Given an input/prompt xx and an action/response yy, the evaluation of yy on xx is assumed to be generated by some latent reward model r∗​(x,y)r^{*}(x,y), which lies in a reward class ℛ\mathcal{R}. For a pair of responses (yw,yl)(y^{w},y^{l}) on xx, human preferences are captured by a theoretical preference model called the Bradley-Terry model [8]. Specifically, given r∗r^{*} being the true reward function, the probability that a response ywy^{w} is preferred over another response yly^{l} on the prompt xx is stipulated as

ℙr∗​(yw≻yl|x)=exp⁡{r∗​(x,yw)}exp⁡{r∗​(x,yw)}+exp⁡{r∗​(x,yl)}=:σ⁡(r∗​(x,yw)−r∗​(x,yl)),\mathbb{P}_{r^{*}}\left(y^{w}\succ y^{l}\big|x\right)=\frac{\exp{\{r^{*}(x,y^{w})\}}}{\exp{\{r^{*}(x,y^{w})\}}+\exp{\{r^{*}(x,y^{l})\}}}=:\sigma\left(r^{*}(x,y^{w})-r^{*}(x,y^{l})\right),

where σ⁡(x)=1/(1+e−x)\sigma(x)=1/(1+e^{-x}) is the logistic function. RLHF/RLAIF methods usually consist of two steps — a reward maximization followed by a policy searching via KL-divergence regularized reinforcement learning. The training preference dataset 𝒮n:={(xi,yiw,yil)}i=1n\mathcal{S}_{n}:=\{(x_{i},y^{w}_{i},y^{l}_{i})\}_{i=1}^{n} is generated according to yw,yl∼πref(⋅|x)y^{w},y^{l}\sim\pi_{\mathrm{ref}}(\cdot|x) where πref\pi_{\mathrm{ref}} is called the reference policy, and the preferences yw≻yly^{w}\succ y^{l} are annotated by human beings/AI. Reward maximization refers to searching a reward function r∈ℛr\in\mathcal{R} to maximize the following likelihood objective

ℒ⁡(r,𝒮n)=𝔼(x,yw,yl)∼𝒮n​[log⁡σ⁡(r⁡(x,yw)−r⁡(x,yl))].\mathcal{L}\left(r,\mathcal{S}_{n}\right)=\mathbb{E}_{(x,y^{w},y^{l})\sim\mathcal{S}_{n}}\left[\log\sigma\left(r(x,y^{w})-r(x,y^{l})\right)\right].

The learned reward function being r^\hat{r} will be used in the next step of RL fine tuning — searching a policy (conditional distribution) π\pi from some policy hypothesis class Π\Pi to maximize the following KL-divergence regularized RL objective

maxπ∈Π{𝔼x∼𝒮n,y∼π(⋅|x)[r^(x,y)]−β⋅𝔻KL(π(y|x)||πref(y|x))},\max_{\pi\in\Pi}\left\{\mathbb{E}_{x\sim\mathcal{S}_{n},y\sim\pi(\cdot|x)}\left[\hat{r}(x,y)\right]-\beta\cdot\mathbb{D}_{\text{KL}}\left(\pi(y|x)\;||\;\pi_{\text{ref}}(y|x)\right)\right\},

where β>0\beta>0 is a hyperparameter to control the weight of the KL-regularizer.

This objective of RLHF/RLAIF has been extensively studied in the past few years [10, 48, 35, 6, 5, 20]. Early works mainly focused on designing efficient RL algorithms such as the Proximal Policy Optimization (PPO) [32] to learn a policy based on a well-estimated reward function. Motivated by the fact that the traditional RLHF pipeline is complex, computationally heavyweight and often unstable, [31] proposed the celebrated Direct Preference Optimization (DPO) algorithm, which directly optimize a policy to adhere to human preferences in a single stage of policy training, without explicit reward modeling. Since then, substantial research effort has shifted toward developing such direct optimization algorithms for various preference learning settings such as iterative/on-policy preference learning [46, 43, 41], active preference learning [25, 12], online/exploratory preference learning [42], and preference learning without using reference model [24]. More recently, motivated by the fact that many reasoning tasks admit rewards that can be automatically checked by programmatic verifiers rather than relying on expensive human-provided preference signals (e.g., verifying the correctness on mathematical problems and code execution), Reinforcement Learning with Verifiable Rewards (RLVR) has been proposed as a variant of RLHF [19, 33, 40]. Unlike in general RLHF where rewards are typically real-valued, RLVR adopts binary rewards — assigning 11 when the generated response passes an automatic verifier and 00 otherwise — which exactly matches our formulation. Therefore, our formulation captures exactly inference-time alignment with verifiable rewards.

Inference-time alignment.

Instead of fine-tuning the language model using the learned reward function as in RLHF, an inference-time alignment algorithm keeps the reference policy πref\pi_{\mathrm{ref}} fixed and uses the reward model only at test time, such as to do rejection sampling [36], to guide decoding token by token [44], to implement planning and search [45], etc. For instance, a canonical inference-time alignment algorithm is the Best-of-NN (BoN) heuristic [36, 15, 7]. Specifically, given an imperfect reward model r^\hat{r} and a new test input xx, BoN works by independently sampling NN candidate responses y(1),…,y(N)y^{(1)},\ldots,y^{(N)} from πref(⋅|x)\pi_{\mathrm{ref}}(\cdot|x), and returns the one with the highest reward of r^\hat{r}, i.e.,

y^BoN​(x)=y(j),where​j∈arg​max1≤i≤N⁡r^​(x,y(i)).\hat{y}_{\mathrm{BoN}}(x)=y^{(j)},\;\;\text{where}\;\;j\in\argmax_{1\leq i\leq N}\hat{r}(x,y^{(i)}).

The imperfect reward model r^\hat{r} can be an open-source reward model or a reward model trained on data separately. As not being the main focus, theoretical works of inference-time alignment usually do not involve analyzing the performance of estimating the true reward function r∗r^{*} by r^\hat{r}, but rather quantifying this estimation error and leave it in bounds. For instance, the estimation quality of r^\hat{r} can be measured by the expected squared error with respect to r∗r^{*} under the reference policy πref\pi_{\mathrm{ref}}, i.e.,

𝔼y∼πref(⋅|x)[(r^(x,y)−r∗(x,y))2].\mathbb{E}_{y\sim\pi_{\mathrm{ref}}(\cdot|x)}\left[\left(\hat{r}(x,y)-r^{*}(x,y)\right)^{2}\right].

In contrast, our learnability result takes both the reward estimation and the test-time computation into consideration since our problem is to learn from scratch — everything should be learned from data without any additional assumptions. Therefore, our theory explains the most general version of inference-time alignment problem. We refer the readers to the work of [15] for a detailed review of inference-time alignment researches.

Learning with multiple correct answers.

Existing theoretical works that are most relevant to ours are perhaps [17, 30]. They both study the same setting as we consider in this work where there are multiple correct answers for an instance, and the learner only needs to output one of them.

Similar to us, [17] studied the problem of language model alignment from a statistical learning perspective. They also assumed that the true reward function r∗r^{*} lies in a low-cardinality reward class ℛ⊆{0,1}𝒳×𝒴\mathcal{R}\subseteq\{0,1\}^{\mathcal{X}\times\mathcal{Y}}.33 3 They further extend their results to ℛ⊆[0,1]𝒳×𝒴\mathcal{R}\subseteq[0,1]^{\mathcal{X}\times\mathcal{Y}}. For simplicity, we discuss here, the case of binary rewards. In their primary setting, the learner receives i.i.d. samples {xi,yi}1≤i≤m\{x_{i},y_{i}\}_{1\leq i\leq m} where each sample contains xi∼𝒟x_{i}\sim\mathcal{D} and yiy_{i} being one of the good responses to the input xix_{i}, i.e., r∗​(xi,yi)=1r^{*}(x_{i},y_{i})=1. Indeed, they assumed that each yiy_{i} is generated from a demonstration policy π~(⋅|xi)\tilde{\pi}(\cdot|x_{i}) supported exactly on the set of good responses given xix_{i}. Denote Vr∗(π)=𝔼x∼𝒟,y∼π(⋅|x)[r∗(x,y)]V_{r^{*}}(\pi)=\mathbb{E}_{x\sim\mathcal{D},y\sim\pi(\cdot|x)}[r^{*}(x,y)]. Their main result is that, with high probability,

Vr∗​(π^)−supπVr∗​(π)=O⁡(log⁡(|ℛ|)m).V_{r^{*}}(\hat{\pi})-\sup_{\pi}V_{r^{*}}(\pi)=O\left(\frac{\log{(|\mathcal{R}|)}}{m}\right).

Their learning algorithm utilizes the classical multiplicative-weights update by maintaining weights over all candidate reward functions and predicting according to their weighted aggregate. Moreover, they also studied a natural extension which they called the pass@kk metric, where the learner still receives training data with a single correct response per sample, but at the test time, the learned policy can output a tuple of responses whose reward is the best reward among the candidates. Under this extension, they improved the convergence rate from O⁡(log⁡(|ℛ|)/m)O(\log(|\mathcal{R}|)/m) to O⁡(logk+1⁡(|ℛ|)/m)O(\log_{k+1}(|\mathcal{R}|)/m).

To clarify our contributions, we list the main difference between our work and theirs as follows. (i) They modeled the problem to also include a policy class in order to exactly match the pipeline of RLHF, while our work models the alignment problem without including a policy class mainly for capturing inference-time alignment methods. (ii) One of the main limitations of their results is that, they restricted to the case where the reward class has a finite cardinality. In contrast, our work provides a complete learnability guarantee for any (infinite) reward class. (iii) They considered that each training sample contains a single correct response, while we assume having multiple responses sampled from the reference policy. We leave the learnability of the single-response model for future works (see our discussion in Section 4). (iv) Finally, their pass@kk extension is the most close to our formulation. However, the success of a learning algorithm in their model only requires that the output tuple at test time contains a good response (which is very close to the list learning44 4 List learning assumes exactly one correct label but their model assumes multiple correct labels. In other words, their learner is expected to output a tuple that intersects with the true label set.), while our definition of success requires to exactly pick out the correct one.

[30] instead considered an online learning variant. They introduced three types of reward feedback models, namely, the mistake-unknown feedback model — after predicting, the learner only sees a correct response but is not told whether its prediction was correct or not, the mistake-known feedback model — the learner is told a correct response as well as the correctness of its prediction, and the set-valued feedback model — the learner sees the entire multiset of correct responses after prediction. They further introduced three generalized versions of the Littlestone dimension [22] to characterize the mistake bound of these three online learning frameworks, respectively.

2 Preliminaries

Throughout the paper, let 𝒳\mathcal{X} be an instance space and 𝒴\mathcal{Y} be an action space. Let ℛ⊆{0,1}𝒳×𝒴\mathcal{R}\subseteq\{0,1\}^{\mathcal{X}\times\mathcal{Y}} be a reward class containing reward functions r:𝒳×𝒴→{0,1}r:\mathcal{X}\times\mathcal{Y}\rightarrow\{0,1\}. Fix some k∈ℕk\in\mathbb{N}. Let 𝒵k=𝒳×𝒴k\mathcal{Z}_{k}=\mathcal{X}\times\mathcal{Y}^{k}. For any reward function r:𝒳×𝒴↦{0,1}r:\mathcal{X}\times\mathcal{Y}\mapsto\{0,1\}, define its induced set-valued acceptance function as Ar:𝒵k↦2[k]A_{r}:\mathcal{Z}_{k}\mapsto 2^{[k]} satisfying Ar​(z)={j∈[k]:r⁡(x,yj)=1}A_{r}(z)=\{j\in[k]:r(x,y_{j})=1\} for any z∈𝒵kz\in\mathcal{Z}_{k}. For a reward class ℛ\mathcal{R}, define its induced set-valued acceptance class as 𝒜k​(ℛ)={Ar:r∈ℛ}\mathcal{A}_{k}(\mathcal{R})=\{A_{r}:r\in\mathcal{R}\}. Our learning problem can be described as follows.

Assume the realizable case where an unknown target reward function r∗∈ℛr^{*}\in\mathcal{R} is to be learned. Let γ∈(0,1)\gamma\in(0,1). Let πref\pi_{\mathrm{ref}} be a conditional distributional measure such that for any x∈𝒳x\in\mathcal{X},

πref(y∈𝒴:r∗(x,y)=1|x)≥γ.\pi_{\mathrm{ref}}(y\in\mathcal{Y}:r^{*}(x,y)=1|x)\geq\gamma.

It is worthwhile to emphasize that we only have oracle (query) access to πref\pi_{\mathrm{ref}}, but have no distribution information of it. For a sample size m∈ℕm\in\mathbb{N}, we collect mm i.i.d. samples,

Sm={(Z1,Ar∗​(Z1)),…,(Zm,Ar∗​(Zm))},S_{m}=\{(Z_{1},A_{r^{*}}(Z_{1})),\ldots,(Z_{m},A_{r^{*}}(Z_{m}))\},

according to the following. Let 𝒟X\mathcal{D}_{X} be some unknown distribution over 𝒳\mathcal{X}. For for every i∈[m]i\in[m], Zi=(Xi,Yi(1),…,Yi(k))∈𝒵kZ_{i}=(X_{i},Y_{i}^{(1)},\ldots,Y_{i}^{(k)})\in\mathcal{Z}_{k} is a random tuple where

Xi∼𝒟XandYi(1),…,Yi(k)∼i.i.d.πref(⋅|Xi).X_{i}\sim\mathcal{D}_{X}\;\;\text{and}\;\;Y_{i}^{(1)},\ldots,Y_{i}^{(k)}\overset{\text{i.i.d.}}{\mathrel{\scalebox{3.0}[1.0]{$\sim$}}}\pi_{\mathrm{ref}}(\cdot|X_{i}). (1)

In brief, each sample contains an instance XiX_{i}, a size-kk slate of labels Yi(1),…,Yi(k)Y_{i}^{(1)},\ldots,Y_{i}^{(k)}, and an acceptance set Ar∗​(Zi)⊆[k]A_{r^{*}}(Z_{i})\subseteq[k] indicating which labels are accepted by the target reward r∗r^{*}. For simplicity, we denote by 𝒟k\mathcal{D}_{k} the distribution over 𝒵k\mathcal{Z}_{k} defined in Equation 1 for a fixed k∈ℕk\in\mathbb{N}. At test time, we are given a test instance X∼𝒟XX\sim\mathcal{D}_{X} accompanied with a size-kk slate of labels Y(1),…,Y(k)Y^{(1)},\ldots,Y^{(k)} i.i.d. generated from πref(⋅|X)\pi_{\mathrm{ref}}(\cdot|X).

The goal is to design a learning algorithm 𝒜\mathcal{A} that takes SmS_{m} as input and outputs a hypothesis 𝒜⁡(Sm):𝒵k→[k]\mathcal{A}(S_{m}):\mathcal{Z}_{k}\rightarrow[k] that, given a test tuple Z=(X,Y(1),…,Y(k))Z=(X,Y^{(1)},\ldots,Y^{(k)}), predicts an index 𝒜⁡(Sm)​(Z)=i^m​(Z)∈[k]\mathcal{A}(S_{m})(Z)=\hat{i}_{m}(Z)\in[k] such that the corresponding response Y(i^m​(Z))Y^{(\hat{i}_{m}(Z))} satisfying r∗​(X,Y(i^m​(Z)))=1r^{*}(X,Y^{(\hat{i}_{m}(Z))})=1 with high probability. Note that this exactly matches the inference-time alignment since the learner selects a good response from candidates rather than predicts one. More formally, we define the learnability of our problem as follows.

Definition 1 (Alignment learnability).

A reward class ℛ\mathcal{R} is called alignment learnable if there exists a learning algorithm 𝒜\mathcal{A} such that, for any γ∈(0,1)\gamma\in(0,1), ϵ∈(0,1)\epsilon\in(0,1) and δ∈(0,1)\delta\in(0,1), there exists k⁡(γ,ϵ,δ)<∞k(\gamma,\epsilon,\delta)<\infty such that, for any k≥k⁡(γ,ϵ,δ)k\geq k(\gamma,\epsilon,\delta), there exists m⁡(k,ϵ,δ)<∞m(k,\epsilon,\delta)<\infty such that, for any m≥m⁡(k,ϵ,δ)m\geq m(k,\epsilon,\delta),

PrZ∼𝒟k[i^m(Z)∈Ar∗(Z)]≥1−ϵ,\Pr_{Z\sim\mathcal{D}_{k}}\left[\hat{i}_{m}(Z)\in A_{r^{*}}(Z)\right]\geq 1-\epsilon,

with probability at least 1−δ1-\delta over the randomness of SmS_{m}.

Remark.

In conclusion, a reward class ℛ\mathcal{R} is alignment learnable if it requires (i) a finite training sample size mm; and (ii) a finite number of inference-time sampling rounds kk. We emphasize that given γ∈(0,1)\gamma\in(0,1) is constant, a finite kk would suffice to guarantee a good response at inference time. The finiteness of the alignment dimension really ensures the finiteness of mm.

2.1 Alignment dimension

We introduce a novel combinatorial dimension, which we call the “alignment dimension”. We show that the alignment dimension of a reward class characterizes its alignment learnability defined in Definition 1.

Definition 2 (Alignment dimension).

Let d∈ℕd\in\mathbb{N}. We say that {x1,…,xd}∈𝒳d\{x_{1},\ldots,x_{d}\}\in\mathcal{X}^{d} are alignment shattered by ℛ\mathcal{R} if there exist (y1(0),y1(1)),…,(yd(0),yd(1))∈(𝒴×𝒴)d(y_{1}^{(0)},y_{1}^{(1)}),\ldots,(y_{d}^{(0)},y_{d}^{(1)})\in(\mathcal{Y}\times\mathcal{Y})^{d} such that for any boolean vector 𝐛∈{0,1}d\bm{b}\in\{0,1\}^{d}, there exists a reward function r𝐛∈ℛr_{\bm{b}}\in\mathcal{R} satisfying that for any i∈[d]i\in[d],

r𝒃​(xi,yi(bi))=1​and​r𝒃​(xi,yi(1−bi))=0.r_{\bm{b}}\left(x_{i},y_{i}^{(b_{i})}\right)=1\;\;\mathrm{and}\;\;r_{\bm{b}}\left(x_{i},y_{i}^{(1-b_{i})}\right)=0.

The alignment dimension of ℛ\mathcal{R}, denoted by dALN​(ℛ)d_{\mathrm{ALN}}(\mathcal{R}), is defined to be the largest d∈ℕd\in\mathbb{N} such that, there exist dd distinct points in 𝒳\mathcal{X} that are alignment shattered by ℛ\mathcal{R}.

Theorem 1.

ℛ\mathcal{R} is alignment learnable if and only if dALN​(ℛ)<∞d_{\mathrm{ALN}}(\mathcal{R})<\infty.

2.2 Examples

In this section, we provide several examples that lead us to the current formulation of the alignment problem, and the one-inclusion-graph algorithm, along with the tournament among non-dominating pairs.

Our first example shows the inherent differences between our learning model and previously well-studied binary classification or multi-class classification. These differences motivate our formulation of the problem, and also rule out several candidates for the learnability characterization.

Definition 3 (VC dimension [39]).

We say that a set {z1=(x1,y1),…,zn=(xn,yn)}\{z_{1}=(x_{1},y_{1}),\ldots,z_{n}=(x_{n},y_{n})\} is shattered by ℛ\mathcal{R}, if for every 𝐛∈{0,1}n\bm{b}\in\{0,1\}^{n}, there exists r𝐛∈ℛr_{\bm{b}}\in\mathcal{R}, such that r𝐛​(zi)=bir_{\bm{b}}(z_{i})=b_{i} for every i∈[n]i\in[n].

The VC dimension of ℛ\mathcal{R} is defined as the largest d∈ℕd\in\mathbb{N} such that there exists a set {z1,…,zd}\{z_{1},\ldots,z_{d}\} shattered by ℛ\mathcal{R}. If no such dd exists, we say that ℛ\mathcal{R} has an infinite VC dimension.

Definition 4 (DS dimension [11]).

Let zi=(xi,yi(1),…,yi(k))z_{i}=(x_{i},y_{i}^{(1)},\ldots,y_{i}^{(k)}). We say that a set {z1,…,zn}\{z_{1},\ldots,z_{n}\} is DS-shattered by 𝒜k​(ℛ)\mathcal{A}_{k}(\mathcal{R}), if for every Ar∈𝒜k​(ℛ)A_{r}\in\mathcal{A}_{k}(\mathcal{R}) and for every i∈[n]i\in[n], there exists Ar′∈𝒜k​(ℛ)A_{r^{\prime}}\in\mathcal{A}_{k}(\mathcal{R}) such that Ar′​(zi)≠Ar​(zi)A_{r^{\prime}}(z_{i})\neq A_{r}(z_{i}) and for every j≠ij\neq i, Ar′​(zj)=Ar​(zj)A_{r^{\prime}}(z_{j})=A_{r}(z_{j}).

The DS dimension of 𝒜k​(ℛ)\mathcal{A}_{k}(\mathcal{R}) is defined as the largest d∈ℕd\in\mathbb{N} such that there exists a set {z1,…,zd}\{z_{1},\ldots,z_{d}\} DS-shattered by 𝒜k​(ℛ)\mathcal{A}_{k}(\mathcal{R}). If no such dd exists, we say that 𝒜k​(ℛ)\mathcal{A}_{k}(\mathcal{R}) has an infinite DS dimension.

A direct approach is to learn a reward function by solving a binary classification problem. This suggests that the VC dimension of ℛ\mathcal{R} might be the characterization of the alignment learnability. Example 1 refutes this conjecture by providing an instance of ℛ\mathcal{R} that has an infinite VC dimension, yet is alignment learnable without any sample. Our second attempt is to reduce the problem to a set-valued multiclass classification problem, where each multiclass classifier Ar∈𝒜k​(ℛ):𝒵k→2[k]A_{r}\in\mathcal{A}_{k}(\mathcal{R}):\mathcal{Z}_{k}\to 2^{[k]}. This means equivalently, for multiple responses to each prompt, to learn exactly which of them are good. It implies that the characterization of the alignment learnability might be the DS dimension of 𝒜k​(ℛ)\mathcal{A}_{k}(\mathcal{R}), which is also falsified by Example 1.

Example 1.

Let Z2={z1=(x1,y1(0),y1(1)),z2=(x2,y2(0),y2(1)),…}Z_{2}=\{z_{1}=(x_{1},y_{1}^{(0)},y_{1}^{(1)}),z_{2}=(x_{2},y_{2}^{(0)},y_{2}^{(1)}),\ldots\}. For every 𝐛∈{0,1}ℕ\bm{b}\in\{0,1\}^{\mathbb{N}}, define r𝐛r_{\bm{b}} according to r𝐛​(xi,yi(0))=1,r𝐛​(xi,yi(1))=bir_{\bm{b}}(x_{i},y_{i}^{(0)})=1,r_{\bm{b}}(x_{i},y_{i}^{(1)})=b_{i}, for every ii. Let ℛ={r𝐛,∀𝐛∈{0,1}ℕ}\mathcal{R}=\{r_{\bm{b}},\forall\bm{b}\in\{0,1\}^{\mathbb{N}}\}.

Note that the reward class ℛ\mathcal{R} defined in Example 1 has an infinite VC dimension since the (infinite) set {(x1,y1(1)),(x2,y2(1)),…}\{(x_{1},y_{1}^{(1)}),(x_{2},y_{2}^{(1)}),\ldots\} is shattered by ℛ\mathcal{R}. Moreover, its induced set-valued acceptance class 𝒜2​(ℛ)\mathcal{A}_{2}(\mathcal{R}) has an infinite DS dimension since the (infinite) set {z1,z2,…}\{z_{1},z_{2},\ldots\} is DS-shattered by 𝒜2​(ℛ)\mathcal{A}_{2}(\mathcal{R}). However, ℛ\mathcal{R} has an alignment dimension dALN​(ℛ)=0d_{\mathrm{ALN}}(\mathcal{R})=0 and is alignment learnable without any training samples using the following strategy. Sample Ω⁡((1/γ)​log⁡(1/ϵ))\Omega((1/\gamma)\log(1/\epsilon)) responses from πref(⋅|x)\pi_{\mathrm{ref}}(\cdot|x) at test time. (This ensures that a good response exists in the pool of candidates. See Section 3.3 for a formal proof.) Then, return y(0)y^{(0)} if it exists and otherwise return y(1)y^{(1)}. This is because, if y(0)y^{(0)} exists, it is always acceptable since all reward functions (including the true reward function) agree that it is good. Otherwise, since at least one good response is in the pool, it must be y(1)y^{(1)}. This suggests that, sampling at test time plays a crucial role in the alignment problem.

Example 1 also justifies that the sample complexity of the Empirical Risk Minimization (ERM) rule, a fundamental algorithmic paradigm in statistical learning, is not characterized by the alignment dimension. Per discussed, we know that dALN​(ℛ)=0d_{\mathrm{ALN}}(\mathcal{R})=0. Moreover, we claim that training an ERM learner on a constant-size sample is insufficient to learn a true reward r∗r^{*}. Consider the case where r∗=r𝟎r^{*}=r_{\mathbf{0}} and the distribution 𝒟\mathcal{D} is uniform over Z2Z_{2}, we know that with probability 11, a test instance does not show up in the sample SmS_{m} for any constant mm. This implies that the worst-case ERM makes a mistake at test time with probability 1/21/2.

While Example 1 admits a simple learning algorithm that does not require any training data but merely relies on test-time sampling, we emphasize that this happens under a special circumstance where the reward class has zero alignment dimension. Our next example gives a reward class with alignment dimension one, showing that only test-time sampling does not suffice and learning from training data is indeed necessary.

Example 2.

Let Z2={z1=(x1,y1(0),y1(1)),z2=(x2,y2(0),y2(1)),…}Z_{2}=\{z_{1}=(x_{1},y_{1}^{(0)},y_{1}^{(1)}),z_{2}=(x_{2},y_{2}^{(0)},y_{2}^{(1)}),\ldots\}, for any i∈ℕi\in\mathbb{N}. For any 𝐛∈{0,1}ℕ\bm{b}\in\{0,1\}^{\mathbb{N}}, define the reward functions r𝐛(10)r^{(10)}_{\bm{b}} and r𝐛(01)r^{(01)}_{\bm{b}} according to

r𝒃(01)​(xi,yi(0))=bi,r𝒃(01)​(xi,yi(1))=1,\displaystyle r^{(01)}_{\bm{b}}(x_{i},y_{i}^{(0)})=b_{i},\;\;r^{(01)}_{\bm{b}}(x_{i},y_{i}^{(1)})=1,
r𝒃(10)​(xi,yi(0))=1,r𝒃(10)​(xi,yi(1))=bi\displaystyle r^{(10)}_{\bm{b}}(x_{i},y_{i}^{(0)})=1,\;\;r^{(10)}_{\bm{b}}(x_{i},y_{i}^{(1)})=b_{i}

for any i∈ℕi\in\mathbb{N}. Now, define a reward class ℛ=ℛ(01)∪ℛ(10)\mathcal{R}=\mathcal{R}^{(01)}\cup\mathcal{R}^{(10)}, where ℛ(10)={r𝐛10,∀𝐛∈{0,1}ℕ}\mathcal{R}^{(10)}=\{r^{10}_{\bm{b}},\forall\bm{b}\in\{0,1\}^{\mathbb{N}}\} and ℛ(01)={r𝐛01,∀𝐛∈{0,1}ℕ}\mathcal{R}^{(01)}=\{r^{01}_{\bm{b}},\forall\bm{b}\in\{0,1\}^{\mathbb{N}}\}. In brief, the reward class ℛ\mathcal{R} realizes all patterns of {11,01}Z2\{11,01\}^{Z_{2}} and {11,10}Z2\{11,10\}^{Z_{2}}.

Note that the reward class ℛ\mathcal{R} in Example 2 has an infinite VC dimension since the (infinite) set {(x1,y1(1)),(x2,y2(1)),…}\{(x_{1},y_{1}^{(1)}),(x_{2},y_{2}^{(1)}),\ldots\} is shattered by ℛ\mathcal{R}. Moreover, we have dALN​(ℛ)=1d_{\mathrm{ALN}}(\mathcal{R})=1 since any reward function cannot realize labels 0101 and 1010 for any two instances. We derive the following conclusions: (1) ℛ\mathcal{R} is not learnable by ERM since this reward class is a superset of the one defined in Example 1; (2) ℛ\mathcal{R} is not learnable relying merely on test-time sampling since any learning algorithm can do no better than a random guess without learning from the training data.

Based on the two examples, it is very likely that to alignment-learn a general reward class ℛ\mathcal{R}, a learning algorithm has to leverage both the training data and test-time sampling. This immediately leads us towards considering the One-Inclusion Graph algorithm. To clarify, our examples do not rule out all the global decision rules, i.e., learners are trained from data and predict immediately at test time (learning is done at training time). What we have shown is that ERM — one of the most natural global decision rules — does not suffice. Therefore, standard inference-time algorithms such as rejection sampling might still be able to achieve alignment learnability, which we leave open for future works.

3 Proof of Theorem 1

In this section, we prove the learnability characterization stated in Theorem 1. The upper bound is proved in Section 3.1-Section 3.3. Specifically, we propose a learning algorithm whose (ϵ,δ)(\epsilon,\delta) sample complexity is bounded in terms of a combinatorial dimension called the “non-dominating Natarajan dimension”. The non-dominating Natarajan dimension is a variant of the classical Natarajan dimension [26, 27] introduced in the context of multiclass classification. We then show that for any reward class, its non-dominating Natarajan dimension is at most its alignment dimension. Altogether, these imply that a finite non-dominating Natarajan dimension suffices to guarantee the alignment learnability. Finally, we prove a matching lower bound in Section 3.4. The lower bound follows from constructing a hard instance directly based on the alignment dimension.

3.1 Non-dominating Natarajan dimension

Definition 5 (Non-dominating Natarajan dimension).

Let k∈ℕk\in\mathbb{N}. Let 𝒵\mathcal{Z} be an instance space. Let 𝒜\mathcal{A} be a set of functions mapping any z∈𝒵z\in\mathcal{Z} to a subset of [k][k]. Let d∈ℕd\in\mathbb{N}. We say that z1,…,zd∈𝒵z_{1},\ldots,z_{d}\in\mathcal{Z} are non-dominating Natarajan shattered by 𝒜\mathcal{A} if there exists (S1(0),S1(1)),…,(Sd(0),Sd(1))∈(2[k]×2[k])d(S_{1}^{(0)},S_{1}^{(1)}),\ldots,(S_{d}^{(0)},S_{d}^{(1)})\in(2^{[k]}\times 2^{[k]})^{d} such that for any i∈[d]i\in[d],

Si(0)≠∅,Si(1)≠∅,Si(0)⊈Si(1)​and​Si(1)⊈Si(0).S_{i}^{(0)}\neq\emptyset,\;\;S_{i}^{(1)}\neq\emptyset,\;\;S_{i}^{(0)}\nsubseteq S_{i}^{(1)}\;\;\mathrm{and}\;\;S_{i}^{(1)}\nsubseteq S_{i}^{(0)}.

And for any boolean vector 𝐛∈{0,1}d\bm{b}\in\{0,1\}^{d}, there exists A𝐛∈𝒜A_{\bm{b}}\in\mathcal{A} such that for any i∈[d]i\in[d],

bi=0⇒A𝒃​(zi)=Si(0)​and​bi=1⇒A𝒃​(zi)=Si(1).b_{i}=0\Rightarrow A_{\bm{b}}(z_{i})=S_{i}^{(0)}\;\;\mathrm{and}\;\;b_{i}=1\Rightarrow A_{\bm{b}}(z_{i})=S_{i}^{(1)}.

The non-dominating Natarajan dimension of 𝒜\mathcal{A}, denoted by dN​(𝒜)d_{\mathrm{N}}(\mathcal{A}), is defined to be the largest d∈ℕd\in\mathbb{N} such that, there exist dd distinct55 5 By saying distinct zz’s, we refer to points zz’s with distinct xx’s in the tuple. points in 𝒵\mathcal{Z} that are non-dominating Natarajan shattered by 𝒜\mathcal{A}.

To see its connection with the standard Natarajan dimension, consider the set-valued class 𝒜\mathcal{A} as an ordinary multiclass concept class consisting of functions mapping an instance z∈𝒵z\in\mathcal{Z} to a subset of [k][k]. The non-dominating Natarajan dimension dN​(𝒜)d_{\mathrm{N}}(\mathcal{A}) is exactly the standard Natarajan dimension of the multiclass class with the constraint that neither of the two reference labels dominates the other. In other words, neither of these two reference labels is a subset of the other.

Specified to our context, let 𝒵=𝒵k\mathcal{Z}=\mathcal{Z}_{k} and 𝒜=𝒜k​(ℛ)\mathcal{A}=\mathcal{A}_{k}(\mathcal{R}). Next, we show that the non-dominating Natarajan dimension of 𝒜k​(ℛ)\mathcal{A}_{k}(\mathcal{R}) is at most the alignment dimension of ℛ\mathcal{R}.

Lemma 1.

For any reward class ℛ⊆{0,1}𝒳×𝒴\mathcal{R}\subseteq\{0,1\}^{\mathcal{X}\times\mathcal{Y}}, we have dN​(𝒜k​(ℛ))≤dALN​(ℛ)d_{\mathrm{N}}(\mathcal{A}_{k}(\mathcal{R}))\leq d_{\mathrm{ALN}}(\mathcal{R}).

Proof.

Suppose that dN​(𝒜k​(ℛ))=dd_{\mathrm{N}}(\mathcal{A}_{k}(\mathcal{R}))=d and z1,…,zd∈𝒵kz_{1},\ldots,z_{d}\in\mathcal{Z}_{k} are non-dominating Natarajan shattered by 𝒜k​(ℛ)\mathcal{A}_{k}(\mathcal{R}). By definition, there are dd pairs of reference label sets (S1(0),S1(1)),…,(Sd(0),Sd(1))(S_{1}^{(0)},S_{1}^{(1)}),\ldots,(S_{d}^{(0)},S_{d}^{(1)}) such that for any boolean vector 𝒃∈{0,1}d\bm{b}\in\{0,1\}^{d}, there exists A𝒃∈𝒜k​(ℛ)A_{\bm{b}}\in\mathcal{A}_{k}(\mathcal{R}) such that for any i∈[d]i\in[d],

bi=0⇒A𝒃​(zi)=Si(0)​and​bi=1⇒A𝒃​(zi)=Si(1).b_{i}=0\Rightarrow A_{\bm{b}}(z_{i})=S_{i}^{(0)}\;\;\text{and}\;\;b_{i}=1\Rightarrow A_{\bm{b}}(z_{i})=S_{i}^{(1)}.

Denote zi=(xi,yi(1),…,yi(k))z_{i}=(x_{i},y_{i}^{(1)},\ldots,y_{i}^{(k)}) for every 1≤i≤d1\leq i\leq d. We show that x1,…,xdx_{1},\ldots,x_{d} are alignment shattered by ℛ\mathcal{R}. Since for any i∈[d]i\in[d],

Since 𝒜k​(ℛ)={Ar:r∈ℛ}\mathcal{A}_{k}(\mathcal{R})=\{A_{r}:r\in\mathcal{R}\}, we have that A𝒃=Ar𝒃A_{\bm{b}}=A_{r_{\bm{b}}} for some r𝒃∈ℛr_{\bm{b}}\in\mathcal{R}. This implies that

bi=0⇒r𝒃​(xi,yi(0))=1,r𝒃​(xi,yi(1))=0b_{i}=0\Rightarrow r_{\bm{b}}\left(x_{i},y_{i}^{(0)}\right)=1,\;r_{\bm{b}}\left(x_{i},y_{i}^{(1)}\right)=0

and

Now, there exists a reward function r𝒃∈ℛr_{\bm{b}}\in\mathcal{R} such that for any i∈[d]i\in[d],

3.2 Learning with finite non-dominating Natarajan dimension

We show that, for any reward class ℛ\mathcal{R}, when the non-dominating Natarajan dimension dN​(𝒜k​(ℛ))d_{\mathrm{N}}(\mathcal{A}_{k}(\mathcal{R})) is finite, ℛ\mathcal{R} is alignment learnable. Our learning algorithm leverages the standard One-inclusion Graph (OIG) algorithm introduced by [14], tailored to learning partial concept classes [1]. Therefore, our final algorithm is in its nature transductive, in the sense that its output hypothesis is not computed explicitly. Rather, given a test point, the learning algorithm uses the training data to predict its label. (In other words, the computation is done at the test time.)

For presenting our algorithm, we introduce several additional notations. For any subset A⊆[k]A\subseteq[k], we define

SA={(z,A):(z,Ar∗(z))∈Sm,Ar∗(z)=A}.S_{A}=\left\{(z,A):(z,A_{r^{*}}(z))\in S_{m},A_{r^{*}}(z)=A\right\}.

We denote by 𝔸OIG​(⋅,⋅)\mathbb{A}_{\mathrm{OIG}}(\cdot;\cdot) the OIG algorithm for learning partial concept classes used in the work of [1]. It takes samples S∈(𝒳×{0,1})∗S\in(\mathcal{X}\times\{0,1\})^{*} as input and predicts 𝔸OIG​(S,x)\mathbb{A}_{\mathrm{OIG}}(S;x) on a test point x∈𝒳x\in\mathcal{X}. Note that while we write the OIG algorithm in terms of {0,1}\{0,1\} labels, it actually works for any binary classification problem. In particular, for two distinct subsets A,B⊆[k]A,B\subseteq[k], S=SA∪SBS=S_{A}\cup S_{B} contains {A,B}\{A,B\} labeled instances, and the OIG algorithm takes SS and predicts 𝔸OIG​(S,z)∈{A,B}\mathbb{A}_{\mathrm{OIG}}(S;z)\in\{A,B\} on a test point z∈𝒵kz\in\mathcal{Z}_{k}. Our learning strategy is formally presented in Figure 1.

For the sake of completeness, we also present how the OIG algorithm works in our problem. To this end, we introduce the following definitions, tailored to our problem setting.

Definition 6 (One-inclusion graph).

Let n∈ℕn\in\mathbb{N}. For a reward class ℛ\mathcal{R} and 𝐳=(z1,…,zn)∈𝒵kn\bm{z}=(z_{1},\ldots,z_{n})\in\mathcal{Z}_{k}^{n}, the induced one-inclusion graph 𝒢⁡(ℛ|𝐳)\mathcal{G}(\mathcal{R}|_{\bm{z}}) is defined as follows. Each vertex it contains is a size-nn tuple representing the “prediction” of a reward function r∈ℛr\in\mathcal{R} on 𝐳\bm{z}, i.e.,

Vr=(Ar​(z1),…,Ar​(zn)).V_{r}=\left(A_{r}(z_{1}),\ldots,A_{r}(z_{n})\right).

For any r∈ℛr\in\mathcal{R} and i∈[n]i\in[n], denote Vr,−i=(Ar​(z1),…,Ar​(zi−1),Ar​(zi+1),…,Ar​(zn))V_{r,-i}=(A_{r}(z_{1}),\ldots,A_{r}(z_{i-1}),A_{r}(z_{i+1}),\ldots,A_{r}(z_{n})). Then, two vertices VrV_{r} and Vr′V_{r^{\prime}} are connected by an edge if there exists i∈[n]i\in[n] such that

Vr,−i=Vr′,−i​and​Ar​(zi)≠Ar′​(zi).V_{r,-i}=V_{r^{\prime},-i}\;\;\text{and}\;\;A_{r}(z_{i})\neq A_{r^{\prime}}(z_{i}).

Accordingly, such an edge is denoted by Er,r′iE_{r,r^{\prime}}^{i}.

Definition 7 (Orientation).

For a one-inclusion graph 𝒢⁡(ℛ|𝐳)\mathcal{G}(\mathcal{R}|_{\bm{z}}), let 𝐕\bm{V} and 𝐄\bm{E} denote the sets of its vertices and edges, respectively. An orientation of 𝒢⁡(ℛ|𝐳)\mathcal{G}(\mathcal{R}|_{\bm{z}}) is a function σ:𝐄↦𝐕\sigma:\bm{E}\mapsto\bm{V} such that for any Er,r′i∈𝐄E_{r,r^{\prime}}^{i}\in\bm{E}, σ⁡(Er,r′i)∈{Vr,Vr′}\sigma(E_{r,r^{\prime}}^{i})\in\{V_{r},V_{r^{\prime}}\}.

Note that for any two nonempty and distinct subsets A,B⊆[k]A,B\subseteq[k], the target acceptance function Ar∗A_{r^{*}} predicts either AA or BB for any zz with (z,Ar∗​(z))∈SA∪SB(z,A_{r^{*}}(z))\in S_{A}\cup S_{B}. However, for an arbitrary r∈ℛr\in\mathcal{R}, ArA_{r} may predict any acceptance subset on such zz. This motivates us to think about a partial concept class 𝒜kA,B(ℛ)={ArA,B:r∈ℛ}⊆{A,B,∗}𝒵k\mathcal{A}^{A,B}_{k}(\mathcal{R})=\{A^{A,B}_{r}:r\in\mathcal{R}\}\subseteq\{A,B,*\}^{\mathcal{Z}_{k}}, where for any r∈ℛr\in\mathcal{R},

ArA,B​(z)={Ar​(z)if​Ar​(z)∈{A,B}∗if​Ar​(z)∉{A,B}.A^{A,B}_{r}(z)=\begin{cases}A_{r}(z)&\text{if}\;\;A_{r}(z)\in\{A,B\}\\ *&\text{if}\;\;A_{r}(z)\notin\{A,B\}\end{cases}.

Let us recall some basic knowledge of partial concept classes. We specify it to our problem for simplicity. For a partial class 𝒜kA,B​(ℛ)\mathcal{A}^{A,B}_{k}(\mathcal{R}), a distribution 𝒟\mathcal{D} over 𝒵k×{A,B}\mathcal{Z}_{k}\times\{A,B\} is called realizable with respect to 𝒜kA,B​(ℛ)\mathcal{A}^{A,B}_{k}(\mathcal{R}) if there exists Ar∗A,B∈𝒜kA,B​(ℛ)A_{r^{*}}^{A,B}\in\mathcal{A}^{A,B}_{k}(\mathcal{R}) (or equivalently, there exists r∗∈ℛr^{*}\in\mathcal{R}) such that z∈supp​(Ar∗A,B)z\in\text{supp}(A_{r^{*}}^{A,B}) for 𝒟\mathcal{D}-almost everywhere zz and the label for zz is Ar∗A,B​(z)A_{r^{*}}^{A,B}(z). Specifically, for any partial hypothesis ArA,B∈𝒜kA,B​(ℛ)A_{r}^{A,B}\in\mathcal{A}^{A,B}_{k}(\mathcal{R}), define its support as

supp(ArA,B)={z∈𝒵k:ArA,B(z)≠∗}.\text{supp}\left(A_{r}^{A,B}\right)=\left\{z\in\mathcal{Z}_{k}:A^{A,B}_{r}(z)\neq*\right\}.

A finite sample {(z1,C1),…,(zn,Cn)}⊆(𝒵k×{A,B})n\{(z_{1},C_{1}),\ldots,(z_{n},C_{n})\}\subseteq(\mathcal{Z}_{k}\times\{A,B\})^{n} is called realizable by 𝒜kA,B​(ℛ)\mathcal{A}^{A,B}_{k}(\mathcal{R}) if there exists some Ar∗A,B∈𝒜kA,B​(ℛ)A_{r^{*}}^{A,B}\in\mathcal{A}^{A,B}_{k}(\mathcal{R}) such that

zi∈supp​(Ar∗A,B)​and​Ar∗A,B​(zi)=Ci,z_{i}\in\text{supp}(A_{r^{*}}^{A,B})\;\;\text{and}\;\;A_{r^{*}}^{A,B}(z_{i})=C_{i},

for every 1≤i≤n1\leq i\leq n. A distribution 𝒟\mathcal{D} over 𝒵k×{A,B}\mathcal{Z}_{k}\times\{A,B\} is called realizable with respect to 𝒜kA,B​(ℛ)\mathcal{A}^{A,B}_{k}(\mathcal{R}) if there exists Ar∗A,B∈𝒜kA,B​(ℛ)A_{r^{*}}^{A,B}\in\mathcal{A}^{A,B}_{k}(\mathcal{R}) such that

Pr(Z,C)∼𝒟⁡(Ar∗A,B​(Z)=C)=1.\Pr_{(Z,C)\sim\mathcal{D}}\left(A_{r^{*}}^{A,B}(Z)=C\right)=1.

and thus every finite sample generated from 𝒟\mathcal{D} is realizable.

Now, suppose that S=SA∪SBS=S_{A}\cup S_{B} have size n∈ℕn\in\mathbb{N}, denoted by

S={(z1,Ar∗​(z1)),…,(zn,Ar∗​(zn))}⊆(𝒵k×{A,B})n.S=\{(z_{1},A_{r^{*}}(z_{1})),\ldots,(z_{n},A_{r^{*}}(z_{n}))\}\subseteq(\mathcal{Z}_{k}\times\{A,B\})^{n}.

It is clear that SS is realizable by 𝒜kA,B​(ℛ)\mathcal{A}^{A,B}_{k}(\mathcal{R}). Let z∈𝒵kz\in\mathcal{Z}_{k} be a test instance and 𝒛=(z1,…,zn,z)\bm{z}=(z_{1},\ldots,z_{n},z). To learn the partial class 𝒜kA,B​(ℛ)\mathcal{A}^{A,B}_{k}(\mathcal{R}), we can simply run the ordinary OIG algorithm on the following total class

𝒜kA,B(ℛ)|𝒛={g:𝒛↦{A,B}n+1:{(zi,g(zi)):1≤i≤n+1} is realizable by 𝒜kA,B(ℛ)}.\mathcal{A}^{A,B}_{k}(\mathcal{R})\big|_{\bm{z}}=\left\{g:\bm{z}\mapsto\{A,B\}^{n+1}:\{(z_{i},g(z_{i})):1\leq i\leq n+1\}\text{ is realizable by }\mathcal{A}^{A,B}_{k}(\mathcal{R})\right\}.

This total class has VC dimension VC⁡(𝒜kA,B​(ℛ)|𝒛)≤VC⁡(𝒜kA,B​(ℛ))\mathrm{VC}(\mathcal{A}^{A,B}_{k}(\mathcal{R})|_{\bm{z}})\leq\mathrm{VC}(\mathcal{A}^{A,B}_{k}(\mathcal{R})), where the VC dimension of a partial concept class is defined the same way as for a total concept class. In the next lemma, we bound VC⁡(𝒜kA,B​(ℛ))\mathrm{VC}(\mathcal{A}^{A,B}_{k}(\mathcal{R})) by the non-domination Natarajan dimension of 𝒜k​(ℛ)\mathcal{A}_{k}(\mathcal{R}).

Lemma 2.

For any two nonempty subsets A,B⊆[k]A,B\subseteq[k] such that A⊈BA\nsubseteq B and B⊈AB\nsubseteq A,

VC⁡(𝒜kA,B​(ℛ))≤dN​(𝒜k​(ℛ)).\mathrm{VC}(\mathcal{A}^{A,B}_{k}(\mathcal{R}))\leq d_{\mathrm{N}}(\mathcal{A}_{k}(\mathcal{R})).
Proof.

The proof follows directly from the definition of the non-dominating Natarajan dimension. Suppose that VC⁡(𝒜kA,B​(ℛ))=d\mathrm{VC}(\mathcal{A}^{A,B}_{k}(\mathcal{R}))=d. Then, there exist z1,…,zd∈𝒵kz_{1},\ldots,z_{d}\in\mathcal{Z}_{k} such that for any boolean vector 𝒃∈{0,1}d\bm{b}\in\{0,1\}^{d}, there exists r𝒃∈ℛr_{\bm{b}}\in\mathcal{R} and thus Ar𝒃A,B∈𝒜kA,B​(ℛ)A_{r_{\bm{b}}}^{A,B}\in\mathcal{A}^{A,B}_{k}(\mathcal{R}) such that

Ar𝒃A,B​(zi)={Aif​bi=0Bif​bi=1A_{r_{\bm{b}}}^{A,B}(z_{i})=\begin{cases}A&\text{if}\;\;b_{i}=0\\ B&\text{if}\;\;b_{i}=1\end{cases}

While the standard OIG algorithm only yields a bound on the expected error rate, [1] combines the one-inclusion predictor with boosting and sample compression to obtain a high probability error rate bound. Therefore, when defining 𝔸OIG​(⋅,⋅)\mathbb{A}_{\mathrm{OIG}}(\cdot;\cdot), we refer to the OIG algorithm followed by boosting and sample compression. Specifically, the following lemma is derived from the results in Appendix C of [1], tailored to our problem setting.

3.3 Upper bound

Combining the results derived in Section 3.1 and Section 3.2, we can show the following result.

Theorem 2.

ℛ\mathcal{R} is alignment learnable if dALN​(ℛ)<∞d_{\mathrm{ALN}}(\mathcal{R})<\infty.

Proof.

By Lemma 1, we know that dN​(𝒜k​(ℛ))≤dALN​(ℛ)d_{\mathrm{N}}(\mathcal{A}_{k}(\mathcal{R}))\leq d_{\mathrm{ALN}}(\mathcal{R}). For any k>0k>0, ϵ∈(0,1)\epsilon\in(0,1) and δ∈(0,1)\delta\in(0,1), define m⁡(k,ϵ,δ)m(k,\epsilon,\delta) as in Lemma 4 by replacing dN​(𝒜k​(ℛ))d_{\mathrm{N}}(\mathcal{A}_{k}(\mathcal{R})) with dALN​(ℛ)d_{\mathrm{ALN}}(\mathcal{R}). It is clear that m⁡(k,ϵ,δ)<∞m(k,\epsilon,\delta)<\infty when dALN​(ℛ)<∞d_{\mathrm{ALN}}(\mathcal{R})<\infty. Moreover, when m>m⁡(k,ϵ,δ)m>m(k,\epsilon,\delta), we know by Lemma 4 that

PrZ∼𝒟k⁡(⋂T∈ΛT⊆Ar∗​(Z)|Ar∗​(Z)≠∅)≥1−ϵ,\Pr_{Z\sim\mathcal{D}_{k}}\left(\bigcap_{T\in\Lambda}T\subseteq A_{r^{*}}(Z)\;\bigg|\;A_{r^{*}}(Z)\neq\emptyset\right)\geq 1-\epsilon,

with probability at least 1−δ1-\delta. Furthermore, note that when Ar∗​(Z)=∅A_{r^{*}}(Z)=\emptyset, our learning procedure has error 11. Now, let

k⁡(γ,ϵ,δ)=Ω⁡(1γ​log⁡(1ϵ)).k(\gamma,\epsilon,\delta)=\Omega\left(\frac{1}{\gamma}\log\left(\frac{1}{\epsilon}\right)\right).

For any k>k⁡(γ,ϵ,δ)k>k(\gamma,\epsilon,\delta), we have by multiplicative Chernoff bound that

PrZ∼𝒟k⁡(Ar∗​(Z)=∅)≤ϵ.\Pr_{Z\sim\mathcal{D}_{k}}\left(A_{r^{*}}(Z)=\emptyset\right)\leq\epsilon.

Suppose that our learning procedure presented in Figure 1 predicts i^m​(Z)∈[k]\hat{i}_{m}(Z)\in[k], we have

PrZ∼𝒟k⁡(i^m​(Z)∉Ar∗​(Z))=\displaystyle\Pr_{Z\sim\mathcal{D}_{k}}\left(\hat{i}_{m}(Z)\notin A_{r^{*}}(Z)\right)= PrZ∼𝒟k⁡(i^m​(Z)∉Ar∗​(Z)|Ar∗​(Z)≠∅)​PrZ∼𝒟k⁡(Ar∗​(Z)≠∅)\displaystyle\Pr_{Z\sim\mathcal{D}_{k}}\left(\hat{i}_{m}(Z)\notin A_{r^{*}}(Z)\;\big|\;A_{r^{*}}(Z)\neq\emptyset\right)\Pr_{Z\sim\mathcal{D}_{k}}\left(A_{r^{*}}(Z)\neq\emptyset\right)
+PrZ∼𝒟k⁡(i^m​(Z)∉Ar∗​(Z)|Ar∗​(Z)=∅)​PrZ∼𝒟k⁡(Ar∗​(Z)=∅)\displaystyle+\Pr_{Z\sim\mathcal{D}_{k}}\left(\hat{i}_{m}(Z)\notin A_{r^{*}}(Z)\;\big|\;A_{r^{*}}(Z)=\emptyset\right)\Pr_{Z\sim\mathcal{D}_{k}}\left(A_{r^{*}}(Z)=\emptyset\right)
≤\displaystyle\leq PrZ∼𝒟k⁡(i^m​(Z)∉Ar∗​(Z)|Ar∗​(Z)≠∅)+PrZ∼𝒟k⁡(Ar∗​(Z)=∅)\displaystyle\Pr_{Z\sim\mathcal{D}_{k}}\left(\hat{i}_{m}(Z)\notin A_{r^{*}}(Z)\;\big|\;A_{r^{*}}(Z)\neq\emptyset\right)+\Pr_{Z\sim\mathcal{D}_{k}}\left(A_{r^{*}}(Z)=\emptyset\right)
≤\displaystyle\leq ϵ+ϵ=2​ϵ,\displaystyle\epsilon+\epsilon=2\epsilon,

with probability at least 1−δ1-\delta. By rescaling ϵ\epsilon, this proves the alignment learnability of ℛ\mathcal{R}. ∎

Finally, we acknowledge that our learning procedure is non-standard in a sense that it implicitly assumes the ordering of the tuple of responses, which is however, permutation invariant. Indeed, for any pair of nonempty subsets A,B⊆[k]A,B\subseteq[k] such that A⊈BA\nsubseteq B and B⊈AB\nsubseteq A, it takes the subsample where each has either AA or BB as the indices of its acceptance set to run the OIG algorithm. It would be interesting to explore a standard learning algorithm that has its sample complexity characterized by the alignment dimension.

3.4 Finishing the proof with a lower bound

In this section, we provide a lower bound, showing that the finiteness of its alignment dimension is also necessary for a reward class to be alignment learnable. The following Theorem 3, together with the upper bound result Theorem 2, finishes the proof of Theorem 1.

Theorem 3.

ℛ\mathcal{R} is alignment learnable only if dALN​(ℛ)<∞d_{\mathrm{ALN}}(\mathcal{R})<\infty.

The next lemma shows that when the alignment dimension of the reward class is infinite, there is a hard instance of distribution such that the reward class is not alignment learnable with finite samples, thus proving Theorem 3.

PrZ∼𝒟⁡(i^m​(Z)∉Ar∗​(Z))≥ϵ,\Pr_{Z\sim\mathcal{D}}\left(\hat{i}_{m}(Z)\notin A_{r^{*}}(Z)\right)\geq\epsilon,

with probability at least δ\delta.

To this end, consider the following distribution 𝒟\mathcal{D} on {z1=(x1,y1(0),y1(1)),z2=(x2,y2(0),y2(1))}\{z_{1}=(x_{1},y_{1}^{(0)},y_{1}^{(1)}),z_{2}=(x_{2},y_{2}^{(0)},y_{2}^{(1)})\}, where z1z_{1} is a shattered point, such that

𝒟⁡(z)={2ϵ,z=z11−2ϵ,z=z2.\mathcal{D}(z)=\begin{cases}2\epsilon,\quad&z=z_{1}\\ 1-2\epsilon,\quad&z=z_{2}\end{cases}.

Now, we define r∗r^{*} as follows. Let r∗​(x2,y2(0))=0r^{*}(x_{2},y_{2}^{(0)})=0, r∗​(x2,y2(1))=1r^{*}(x_{2},y_{2}^{(1)})=1. It follows that with probability 1/21/2, r∗​(x1,y1(0))=0r^{*}(x_{1},y_{1}^{(0)})=0, r∗​(x1,y1(1))=1r^{*}(x_{1},y_{1}^{(1)})=1, and with probability 1/21/2, r∗​(x1,y1(0))=1r^{*}(x_{1},y_{1}^{(0)})=1, r∗​(x1,y1(1))=0r^{*}(x_{1},y_{1}^{(1)})=0. Notice that in this case, if the event that SmS_{m} does not contain z1z_{1}, denoted by ℰ′\mathcal{E}^{\prime}, occurs, any learning algorithm will predict wrong on z1z_{1}, with probability 1/21/2. Putting together, we have

𝔼Z∼𝒟,r∗[𝟙[i^m(Z)∉Ar∗(Z)]|ℰ′]=12⋅2ϵ=ϵ.\mathbb{E}_{Z\sim\mathcal{D},r^{*}}\left[\left.\mathbbm{1}\left[\hat{i}_{m}(Z)\notin A_{r^{*}}(Z)\right]\right|\mathcal{E}^{\prime}\right]=\frac{1}{2}\cdot 2\epsilon=\epsilon.

Hence, there exists a deterministic r∗r^{*} such that PrZ∼𝒟⁡(i^m​(Z)∉Ar∗​(Z)|ℰ′)=ϵ\Pr_{Z\sim\mathcal{D}}(\hat{i}_{m}(Z)\notin A_{r^{*}}(Z)|\mathcal{E}^{\prime})=\epsilon. Then we only need to show that Pr⁡(ℰ′)≥δ\Pr(\mathcal{E}^{\prime})\geq\delta. Since SmS_{m} is i.i.d. sampled from the distribution 𝒟\mathcal{D}, we have Pr⁡(ℰ′)=(1−2​ϵ)m\Pr(\mathcal{E}^{\prime})=(1-2\epsilon)^{m}. Since 0<ϵ<1/600<\epsilon<1/60, we further have 1−2​ϵ>1−4​ϵ+16​ϵ2>e−4​ϵ1-2\epsilon>1-4\epsilon+16\epsilon^{2}>e^{-4\epsilon}, which yields that Pr⁡(ℰ′)=(1−2​ϵ)m>e−4​ϵ​m=eln⁡(δ)=δ\Pr(\mathcal{E}^{\prime})=(1-2\epsilon)^{m}>e^{-4\epsilon m}=e^{\ln(\delta)}=\delta. ∎

4 Discussion

We formulate the problem of inference-time alignment into a statistical learning framework, where the goal is to boost the prediction performance of a reference policy by leveraging the preference data. We define the notion of alignment learnability in a sense of weak-to-strong learning: given a reference policy (weak predictor), is there a finite sample size such that i.i.d. training data can be used to produce a strong predictor that predicts good response with arbitrarily high probability at test time? We seek for a characterization of alignment learnability — asking which reward classes are alignment learnable. As a pioneering work, we restrict to the realizable case as well as binary rewards. We introduce a novel and natural combinatorial dimension of the reward class called the alignment dimension, which provides a complete characterization of the alignment learnability — a reward class is alignment learnable if and only if its alignment dimension is finite. We notice that our learning procedure is non-standard in a sense that it additionally assumes the ordering of the response tuple, which is however, permutation invariant.

We consider our work as an initial step towards establishing a general statistical learning theory for alignment. Since we just figured out its learnability, a natural follow-up question is to quantify the optimal sample complexity required to achieve the (γ,ϵ,δ)(\gamma,\epsilon,\delta) alignment learnability, namely, the optimal dependencies in terms of γ\gamma, ϵ\epsilon and δ\delta. Moreover, we notice that our learning model differs from existing frameworks such as multiclass learning and list learning, and itself might be of independent interests to the learning theory community. Indeed, various extensions such as online learning and active learning could be interesting to study. The following problems are those more closely related to our formulation.

4.1 Learning with single-response training data

One of the main constraints of our theory is that, we assume having multiple responses y(1),…,y(k)y^{(1)},\ldots,y^{(k)} sampled from the reference policy πref(⋅|x)\pi_{\mathrm{ref}}(\cdot|x) for each input xx. This assumption arises from a technical reason. Since the reference policy has a constant probability of outputting a good response, having multiple responses sampled aims to ensure that there exists a good response within the generated tuple. In particular, having multiple responses at test time is necessary, since the learner is expected to select a response from the test slate. This leads to its necessity also in the training data generation since our learning procedure invokes the leave-one-out one-inclusion graph algorithm, which relies on the exchangeability of training and test instances.

On the other hand, in practical language model alignment tasks, usually only two responses are collected for each prompt to be compared by human annotators. This motivates the following open problem: which reward classes are alignment learnable with single-response training data (and of course we still collect multiple responses at test time). Note that for binary rewards, having one or two responses makes almost no difference, since in both cases the event that all sampled responses have reward values 00 or 11 happens with constant probability. We conjecture that our alignment dimension might also characterize the “single-response” alignment learnability.

4.2 Learning to predict rather than to select

Another constraint of our formulation is that the learner is expected to select a good response from multiple candidates. However, practical alignment methods, especially RLHF methods, instead seek to predict a good response for a given test prompt.66 6 Note that this does not necessarily require to learn a policy from a hypothesis policy class. More formally, under the setting of Section 2, the goal is then to design a learning algorithm 𝒜\mathcal{A} that takes SmS_{m} as input and outputs a predictor 𝒜⁡(Sm):𝒳→𝒴\mathcal{A}(S_{m}):\mathcal{X}\rightarrow\mathcal{Y} that, given a test instance X∼𝒟XX\sim\mathcal{D}_{X}, predicts a response Y^=𝒜⁡(Sm)​(X)∈𝒴\hat{Y}=\mathcal{A}(S_{m})(X)\in\mathcal{Y} such that r∗​(X,Y^)=1r^{*}(X,\hat{Y})=1 with high probability.

While it might be interesting to have a theoretical understanding towards this learning model, it is worth mentioning that this formulation mismatches practical alignment in a sense that, the learner’s prediction is irrelevant to the reference policy πref\pi_{\mathrm{ref}}. However, for practical alignment such as RLHF approaches, a regularization of KL-divergence 𝔻KL(⋅||πref(y|x))\mathbb{D}_{\text{KL}}(\cdot||\pi_{\mathrm{ref}}(y|x)) is usually appended to a policy optimization objective to ensure that the learned policy (predictor) stays close to the reference policy and thus may inherit nice properties from it such as linguistic fluency and broad knowledge. It is also for this reason we study the selection-based prediction in this work.

4.3 Learning with preferences

A more significant and challenging extension is to study exactly alignment with preferences. Specifically, consider the setting of real-valued rewards, for example, ℛ∈[0,1]𝒳×𝒴\mathcal{R}\in[0,1]^{\mathcal{X}\times\mathcal{Y}}. Every training sample consists of an prompt x∈𝒳x\in\mathcal{X}, two independent responses y(0),y(1)y^{(0)},y^{(1)} generated from the reference policy πref(⋅|x)\pi_{\mathrm{ref}}(\cdot|x), and a boolean remark σ=𝟙[y(0)≻y(1)]\sigma=\mathbbm{1}[y^{(0)}\succ y^{(1)}] indicating which response is more preferred according to the true reward function r∗∈ℛr^{*}\in\mathcal{R}. This setting could be considered as an offline variant of dueling bandits. Given i.i.d. samples Sm={(xi,yi(0),yi(1),σi)}i=1mS_{m}=\{(x_{i},y_{i}^{(0)},y_{i}^{(1)},\sigma_{i})\}_{i=1}^{m}, the learner 𝒜\mathcal{A} is expected to predict a response 𝒜​(Sm)​(x)∈𝒴\mathcal{A}(S_{m})(x)\in\mathcal{Y} on a test prompt xx such that

Prx∼𝒟X,y′∼πref(⋅|x)(𝒜(Sm)(x)≻y′)≥1−ϵ.\Pr_{x\sim\mathcal{D}_{X},y^{\prime}\sim\pi_{\mathrm{ref}}(\cdot|x)}\left(\mathcal{A}(S_{m})(x)\succ y^{\prime}\right)\geq 1-\epsilon.

with probability at least 1−δ1-\delta.

The challenge arises as how to measure the quality of the reference policy. [15] made an assumption on the reference policy’s coverage. They defined the coverage coefficient as

𝒞π∗(x)=𝔼y∼π∗(⋅|x)[π∗​(y|x)πref​(y|x)]\mathcal{C}^{\pi^{*}}(x)=\mathbb{E}_{y\sim\pi^{*}(\cdot|x)}\left[\frac{\pi^{*}(y|x)}{\pi_{\mathrm{ref}}(y|x)}\right]

where π∗\pi^{*} is a comparator policy that achieves high true rewards, and assumed that 𝒞π∗​(x)≤C\mathcal{C}^{\pi^{*}}(x)\leq C for some constant C>0C>0 holds uniformly for any xx. [34] proposed another measure of discrepancy between πref\pi_{\mathrm{ref}} and π∗\pi^{*} called the ℰM\mathcal{E}_{M}-divergence. [47] studied other coverage conditions including the Global-Policy Coverage and the Local KL-ball Coverage. Note that such assumptions are usually formulated as discrepancy measures between πref\pi_{\mathrm{ref}} and a comparator policy. Instead, can we model the reference policy assumption to only rely on parameters γ\gamma, ϵ\epsilon and δ\delta?

Instructions for reporting errors

We are continuing to improve HTML versions of papers, and your feedback helps enhance accessibility and mobile support. To report errors in the HTML that will help us improve conversion and rendering, choose any of the methods listed below:

Tip: You can select the relevant text first, to include it in your report.

Our team has already identified the following issues. We appreciate your time reviewing and reporting rendering errors we may not have found yet. Your efforts will help us improve the HTML versions for all readers, because disability should not be a barrier to accessing research. Thank you for your continued support in championing open access for all.
